_note: “Did you know?” box on the printable sheet of a word set (src/pages/vocabulary/print/[set].astro): two or three short facts about French and life in France, tied to the words of the unit, in the English of the level. Keys are the set ids a1-01 to b2-60. Machine draft 2026-11-12, not yet reviewed by a teacher; figures and institutions are general orientation (check the official site).
a1-01: In French you say your age with ‘avoir’: ‘J'ai trente ans’ means ‘I have thirty years’.
Phone numbers in France have ten digits and are said in pairs: 06 12 34 56 78 is ‘zéro six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit’.
Dates are written day / month / year: 12/11/2026 is the twelfth of November, not the eleventh of December.
a1-02: ‘Un parent’ can mean ‘a relative’, not only a mother or father. ‘Mes parents’ means ‘my parents’.
‘Mon’, ‘ma’, ‘mes’ agree with the noun, not with the owner. Before a vowel you use ‘mon’ even for a woman: ‘mon amie’, ‘mon école’.
At home most children say ‘papa’ and ‘maman’, also when they are adults. For grandparents you often hear ‘mamie’ and ‘papi’.
a1-03: ‘Problème’ ends in -e but is masculine: ‘un problème’, not ‘une problème’.
French uses ‘avoir’ for many feelings: ‘J'ai peur’ (I am afraid), ‘J'ai envie de…’ (I feel like…).
‘J'adore’ is very common for things you like: ‘J'adore le fromage’. ‘Je t'aime’ to a person is much stronger.
a1-04: Flats are described by their number of rooms: ‘un trois-pièces’ has three rooms, usually without the kitchen and the bathroom.
‘Le rez-de-chaussée’ is the ground floor. ‘Le premier étage’ is the floor above it, so it is one floor up.
‘Une chambre’ is a bedroom, not any room. The toilet is often a separate room: ‘les toilettes’ or ‘les WC’.
a1-05: ‘Un meuble’ is one piece of furniture. ‘Des meubles’ means several pieces; for furniture in general you say ‘le mobilier’.
‘Le frigo’ is short for ‘le réfrigérateur’. Many people also say ‘le frigidaire’, which was once a brand name.
A double bed is ‘un lit deux places’, a single bed ‘un lit une place’.
a1-06: ‘Eau’ is feminine, and for an amount you say ‘de l'eau’. With ‘du pain’, ‘de la viande’, ‘de l'eau’ you say ‘some’.
In a French café ‘un café’ is a small, strong black coffee. For milk, ask for ‘un café crème’ or ‘un café au lait’.
‘Un œuf’ is said [œf], but ‘des œufs’ is said [ø]: the -f disappears in the plural.
a1-07: Prices are written with a comma and the euro sign after the number: 2,50 €. You say ‘deux euros cinquante’.
At the till ask for or keep ‘le ticket de caisse’ (the receipt). You need it if you want to return something.
Free thin plastic bags are no longer given out in shops, so many people bring their own bag.
a1-08: Colours agree with the noun: ‘une robe verte’, ‘des chaussures noires’. But ‘orange’ and ‘marron’ never change: ‘des chaussures marron’.
For clothes you ask for your ‘taille’ (for example 38 or 40). For shoes you ask for your ‘pointure’.
‘Un pantalon’ is singular in French: ‘Ce pantalon est trop grand’ means ‘These trousers are too big’.
a1-09: To say where it hurts, use ‘avoir mal à’: ‘J'ai mal à la tête’, ‘J'ai mal au dos’, ‘J'ai mal aux pieds’.
‘Un œil’ becomes ‘des yeux’ in the plural. ‘Les cheveux’ (hair) is nearly always plural.
With parts of the body French often uses ‘le’, ‘la’, ‘les’, not ‘my’: ‘Je me lave les mains’.
a1-10: In an emergency call 15 (the SAMU, medical help) or 112, the European number. 17 is the police and 18 the fire brigade.
Your ‘médecin traitant’ is the doctor you name to the health insurance as your main doctor. Visits are reimbursed better if you go through them.
Your ‘carte Vitale’ is the green health-insurance card. Many people book doctor's appointments online, for example on Doctolib.
a1-11: In France ‘déjeuner’ is lunch and ‘dîner’ is dinner. In Québec, Belgium and Switzerland ‘déjeuner’ is breakfast, ‘dîner’ is lunch and ‘souper’ is dinner.
‘Se lever’ is a reflexive verb: ‘Je me lève à sept heures’. The ‘me’ is part of the verb.
Times are written with ‘h’: 19 h 30. In writing the 24-hour clock is common, and in speech people use both.
a1-12: After ‘être’ you do not use ‘un’ or ‘une’ for a job: ‘Je suis cuisinier’, ‘Elle est professeure’.
Many job names change for women: ‘un serveur, une serveuse’, ‘un infirmier, une infirmière’. Others stay the same: ‘un collègue, une collègue’.
‘Le travail’ is work, but its plural ‘les travaux’ means building or road works.
a1-13: ‘L'école’ usually means primary school. Pupils then go to ‘le collège’ and ‘le lycée’.
Gender trap: ‘un livre’ is a book, but ‘une livre’ is a pound (weight or money).
‘Passer un examen’ means to take an exam, not to pass it. To pass it you say ‘réussir un examen’.
School exercise books have lines in a fine grid called ‘Seyès’, which is typical of France.
a1-14: Sports with a ball use ‘jouer à’ (‘jouer au foot’). Music uses ‘jouer de’ (‘jouer du piano’). Other activities use ‘faire du’: ‘faire du vélo’.
The ‘Fête de la musique’ is every year on 21 June. People play and sing in the streets, and most concerts are free.
‘Le foot’ is short for ‘le football’. Many French people also play ‘la pétanque’, a game with metal balls.
a1-15: ‘La mairie’ is the town hall. You go there for many papers, and weddings take place there. The French flag hangs outside.
In cities the police station is ‘le commissariat’. In villages and the countryside you go to ‘la gendarmerie’.
False friend: a library is ‘une bibliothèque’. ‘Une librairie’ is a bookshop.
a1-16: Prepositions with transport: ‘en train’, ‘en bus’, ‘en voiture’, but ‘à pied’ and ‘à vélo’.
A ‘billet’ is a train or plane ticket. For the métro and bus you often hear ‘un ticket’. The first Paris métro line opened in 1900.
On a station board you look for the ‘voie’ (the track number) of your train, and the ‘quai’ is the platform.
a1-17: ‘Vacances’ is always plural: ‘les vacances’, ‘de bonnes vacances’. You say ‘Bonnes vacances !’.
‘La carte’ means a card, a map and the restaurant menu list. Context tells you which.
By law employees in France get five weeks of paid holiday a year (‘congés payés’).
a1-18: 70 is ‘soixante-dix’, 80 is ‘quatre-vingts’, 90 is ‘quatre-vingt-dix’. In Belgium and Switzerland you also hear ‘septante’ and ‘nonante’.
Days and months are not written with a capital letter: ‘lundi’, ‘mardi’, ‘janvier’. ‘Le lundi’ means ‘every Monday’.
Only the first day of the month is an ordinal: ‘le premier mai’, but ‘le deux mai’, ‘le trois mai’.
a1-19: ‘Le temps’ means weather and also time. ‘Quel temps fait-il ?’ asks about the weather.
French uses ‘faire’ for the weather: ‘Il fait beau’, ‘Il fait froid’, ‘Il fait 20 degrés’. But rain and snow are verbs: ‘Il pleut’, ‘Il neige’.
Seasons: ‘au printemps’ but ‘en été’, ‘en automne’, ‘en hiver’.
a1-20: The plural of ‘cheval’ is ‘chevaux’ and of ‘animal’ is ‘animaux’: -al becomes -aux.
‘Une poule’ is a hen, ‘un coq’ a cock, and ‘du poulet’ is chicken as food.
People often use animal names as sweet words: ‘mon chat’, ‘ma puce’ (my flea), ‘mon chou’ (my cabbage).
a1-21: ‘Il y a’ means ‘there is’ and ‘there are’, and it never changes: ‘Il y a un chat’, ‘Il y a deux chats’. With a time it means ‘ago’: ‘il y a deux ans’.
‘Voir’ is to see, ‘regarder’ is to look at. ‘Entendre’ is to hear, ‘écouter’ is to listen to.
Irregular forms to learn early: ‘vous dites’, not ‘vous disez’; ‘vous faites’, not ‘vous faisez’.
a1-22: ‘Je voudrais’ is the polite way to ask: ‘Je voudrais un café.’ ‘Je veux un café’ sounds more direct.
‘Savoir’ is for facts and skills (‘Je sais nager’). ‘Connaître’ is for people and places (‘Je connais Paul’).
‘Devoir’ means ‘must’ and also ‘to owe’: ‘Je te dois dix euros’. ‘Les devoirs’ is homework.
a1-23: Short common adjectives often come before the noun: ‘une petite maison’, ‘un bon repas’, ‘un nouveau film’. Most others come after: ‘une voiture rapide’.
Before a vowel some adjectives change: ‘un nouvel ami’, ‘un bel homme’, ‘un vieil homme’.
In the feminine the last consonant is heard: ‘grand’ sounds like ‘gran’, ‘grande’ sounds like ‘grand’.
a1-24: ‘Chez’ means ‘at the home of’: ‘chez moi’, ‘chez Paul’, ‘chez le médecin’.
‘À’ and ‘de’ join with ‘le’ and ‘les’: ‘au parc’, ‘aux toilettes’, ‘à côté du parc’, ‘près des magasins’.
Countries: ‘en France’, ‘en Italie’ (feminine or vowel), ‘au Maroc’ (masculine), ‘aux États-Unis’ (plural).
a1-25: ‘Parce que’ becomes ‘parce qu'’ before a vowel: ‘parce qu'il pleut’. ‘Si’ also changes before ‘il’: ‘s'il pleut’, but ‘si elle pleure’.
‘Ou’ (or) and ‘où’ (where) sound the same. Only the accent shows the difference. The same is true of ‘a’ (has) and ‘à’ (to).
‘Quel’ agrees with the noun: ‘quel livre’, ‘quelle heure’, ‘quels films’, ‘quelles questions’.
a1-26: On a form ‘Nom’ is your family name and ‘Prénom’ is your first name. Do not mix them up.
A French postcode has five digits. The first two usually show the département: 75 is Paris, 13 is Bouches-du-Rhône (Marseille).
On contracts people often write ‘lu et approuvé’ by hand before the signature. Official forms stopped using ‘Mademoiselle’ in 2012.
a2-01: In ads ‘F2’ or ‘T2’ means a flat with a living room and one bedroom. ‘Vide’ means unfurnished, ‘meublé’ furnished.
‘CC’ means ‘charges comprises’ (service costs included in the rent) and ‘HC’ means ‘hors charges’ (not included). Always check which.
The deposit (‘dépôt de garantie’) is usually one month's rent for an unfurnished flat and up to two months for a furnished one. Check the contract.
a2-02: Many people say ‘bonjour’ to neighbours in the stairs or the lift, even if they do not know them well.
In many places there is a ‘Fête des voisins’ in late May or early June, when residents meet and eat together.
Night noise (‘tapage nocturne’) is an offence, usually from about 10 pm to 6 am. Local rules can differ.
a2-03: French uses ‘faire’ for housework: ‘faire la vaisselle’, ‘faire le ménage’, ‘faire la lessive’, ‘faire les courses’.
‘Bricoler’ means doing small DIY jobs at home. ‘Le bricolage’ is a very popular hobby.
‘Repasser’ means to iron, but it also means to pass or come by again.
a2-04: After an amount you use ‘de’ without the article: ‘un kilo de farine’, ‘un peu d'huile’, ‘pas de sel’.
False friend: ‘le poivre’ is the spice, ‘un poivron’ is a pepper (a vegetable).
Recipes often use the infinitive for instructions: ‘Couper les oignons. Ajouter le sel.’
a2-05: Prices on French menus include service (‘service compris’). A tip is not required. Many people leave a few coins.
‘Le menu’ is a set meal at a fixed price. The list of dishes is ‘la carte’. ‘Une formule’ is usually a starter and main course, or a main course and dessert.
A jug of tap water (‘une carafe d'eau’) is normally free. You have to ask for ‘l'addition’; it is not brought on its own.
a2-06: ‘Se casser le bras’ uses ‘le’, not ‘mon’: ‘Je me suis cassé le bras’.
Other common ‘avoir mal’ phrases: ‘J'ai mal à la gorge’, ‘J'ai mal au ventre’, ‘Il a de la fièvre’.
A usual visit to a doctor costs around thirty euros and the health insurance pays back part of it. Check ameli.fr for the current price.
a2-07: Medicines are sold in pharmacies (green cross). Even common painkillers are usually kept behind the counter, so you can ask the pharmacist for advice.
‘Une notice’ is the leaflet in the box. For a prescription you say ‘une ordonnance’.
A ‘cachet’ is a pill, ‘un comprimé’ a tablet, ‘une gélule’ a capsule. At night and on Sundays look for the ‘pharmacie de garde’.
a2-08: With body care French does not use ‘my’: ‘Je me brosse les dents’, ‘Je me lave les cheveux’.
‘Une brosse à dents’ and ‘un sèche-cheveux’ show typical compounds: ‘à’ or a verb plus a noun.
‘Le savon de Marseille’ is a famous traditional soap, often sold as a green or white cube.
a2-09: A French CV is often one page. You do not have to add a photo, and age or marital status are not needed.
‘Le SMIC’ is the legal minimum wage. The government reviews it at least once a year, on 1 January.
Letters usually end with a long polite formula, for example ‘Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.’ In an email ‘Cordialement’ is enough.
a2-10: The legal working week for full-time work is 35 hours. Hours beyond that are ‘heures supplémentaires’.
Many employers give ‘titres-restaurant’ (meal vouchers) or a ‘cantine’ and pay part of the lunch.
‘Responsable’ means ‘manager’ as well as ‘responsible’: ‘la responsable de l'équipe’.
a2-11: ‘Le bac’ is short for ‘le baccalauréat’, the exam at the end of the lycée. ‘Avoir son bac’ means to have passed it.
‘Faire la connaissance de quelqu'un’ means to meet someone for the first time. ‘Une connaissance’ is also an acquaintance.
Working people have a personal training account called ‘CPF’ (compte personnel de formation). Check moncompteformation.gouv.fr.
a2-12: Employers and landlords often ask for your ‘RIB’ (relevé d'identité bancaire), the paper with your IBAN.
‘Une pièce’ has many meanings: a coin, a room, a play, a document (‘une pièce d'identité’).
Cheques still exist in France, but most people pay by card or ‘virement’ (transfer) and ‘prélèvement’ (direct debit).
a2-13: For official letters people use ‘une lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception’: you get proof that it was delivered.
Foreign residents have a ‘titre de séjour’. People also say ‘carte de séjour’. Keep the ‘récépissé’ (receipt) when your card is being renewed.
France has no registration at the town hall. Instead many offices ask for a ‘justificatif de domicile’, for example an electricity or internet bill of the last three months.
a2-14: A home insurance (‘assurance habitation’) is required for tenants. A car must have at least liability insurance.
After an accident both drivers fill in a ‘constat amiable’, now often with an app. It is not a police report.
‘L'assurance maladie’ is the public health insurance. The private extra insurance is called ‘la mutuelle’.
a2-15: On the phone say ‘Bonjour, je voudrais parler à…’. ‘Ne quittez pas’ means ‘please hold’. Mobile numbers begin with 06 or 07.
In an email address ‘@’ is ‘arobase’, ‘.’ is ‘point’, ‘-’ is ‘tiret’ and ‘_’ is ‘tiret bas’.
‘Courriel’ is the official word for email and is common in Québec. In France people usually say ‘un mail’.
a2-16: French keyboards are AZERTY, not QWERTY. The letters A and Z, and Q and W, swap places, and M is in a different place.
‘FranceConnect’ lets you use one login for many state websites, for example the tax office or ameli.
‘Un portable’ is a mobile phone. A laptop is ‘un ordinateur portable’.
a2-17: New goods have a legal guarantee (‘garantie légale de conformité’), usually two years.
For online purchases you usually have 14 days to change your mind (‘droit de rétractation’).
‘Un avoir’ is a credit note: a shop gives you credit instead of money back. If you want a refund say ‘un remboursement’.
a2-18: On a train the carriage is ‘la voiture’, not ‘le wagon’. A TGV ticket shows ‘voiture 12, place 34’, and a seat is always reserved on a TGV.
Strikes in transport are announced in advance. The SNCF app and site show if ‘le trafic est perturbé’.
In Paris and the region many people use a Navigo pass instead of single tickets.
a2-19: ‘Priorité à droite’: at a junction without signs, a car coming from the right has priority. It is a typical trap for newcomers.
French licences work with points: a full licence starts with 12 points and you lose points for offences.
Many motorways (‘autoroutes’) have tolls (‘péage’). You can pay by card at the barrier.
a2-20: ‘Un gîte’ is a holiday cottage you rent for yourself. ‘Une chambre d'hôtes’ is a room in a private house with breakfast.
Breakfast is often not included in the hotel price: ‘petit-déjeuner en supplément’.
Hotels add a small tourist tax (‘taxe de séjour’) per person and per night.
a2-21: ‘Le réveillon’ is the festive meal on the evening of 24 December and again on 31 December.
On 6 January many people eat ‘la galette des Rois’. Whoever finds the ‘fève’ (a small figure) in their slice is king or queen.
On 14 July, the national day, there are fireworks and a military parade in Paris. ‘Félicitations !’ always has a final -s.
a2-22: For sports French uses ‘jouer à’ for ball games (‘jouer au tennis’) and ‘faire du’ for others (‘faire du judo’).
The Tour de France, the cycling race, takes place every July. The tennis tournament Roland-Garros is in Paris in May and June.
‘Un but’ is a goal. The -t is pronounced: ‘but’ sounds like ‘byt’.
a2-23: In cinemas ‘VF’ is the French version (dubbed) and ‘VO’ or ‘VOST’ the original version with subtitles.
French radio stations have to play a share of songs in French. The law fixes a quota of around 40 per cent for many stations.
‘Un morceau’ is a piece: a piece of music or a piece of cake. ‘Une pièce de théâtre’ is a play.
a2-24: Many adjectives change in the feminine: ‘gentil → gentille’, ‘paresseux → paresseuse’, ‘travailleur → travailleuse’, ‘sportif → sportive’.
‘Sympathique’ means ‘nice, pleasant’, not ‘sympathetic’. In daily speech people say ‘sympa’, for men and women.
‘Bête’ is an adjective (stupid, a mild word) and a noun (‘une bête’, an animal).
a2-25: ‘Préférer’ changes the accent: ‘je préfère’, but ‘nous préférons’. The accent grave only comes where the ending is silent.
Many feminine forms look different but sound the same: ‘fâché, fâchée’, ‘ravi, ravie’, ‘fier, fière’.
‘Gêné’ means embarrassed (‘Je suis gêné’). ‘Ça ne me dérange pas’ means ‘I don't mind’.
a2-26: In most towns plastic, metal, paper and cardboard go into the ‘bac jaune’ (the yellow bin). Glass goes into a glass container, ‘le conteneur à verre’.
The ‘Triman’ logo on packaging shows that the product should be sorted for recycling.
A bin is called ‘une poubelle’ after Eugène Poubelle, a prefect of Paris who ordered bins in 1884.
a2-27: Reflexive verbs use ‘être’ in the perfect tense: ‘Je me suis trompé(e)’, ‘Elle s'est dépêchée’.
In the imperative the pronoun comes after: ‘Dépêche-toi !’, ‘Dépêchez-vous !’, but ‘Ne te dépêche pas !’.
‘Se rendre compte’ means to realise: ‘Je me rends compte que j'ai oublié mes clés’.
a2-28: ‘Je veux’ can sound too direct. ‘Je voudrais’ and ‘J'aimerais’ are polite.
In speech people often use ‘on’ for ‘nous’: ‘On y va ?’ (Shall we go?), ‘On se retrouve devant la gare ?’.
A question can just go up at the end: ‘Tu viens ?’. Use ‘s'il te plaît’ with ‘tu’ and ‘s'il vous plaît’ with ‘vous’.
b1-01: ‘CDI’ is the open-ended contract and ‘CDD’ the fixed-term one. A trial period (‘période d'essai’) is usually two to four months, depending on the job category.
If you resign (‘démission’), you usually do not get unemployment benefit. There are some exceptions.
Collective agreements (‘conventions collectives’) set rules for a whole sector. The name of yours is on your payslip.
b1-02: Your ‘médecin traitant’ is the first contact. If you see a specialist without being referred, you are usually reimbursed less.
Physiotherapy (‘kiné’, short for ‘kinésithérapie’) is usually prescribed by a doctor, and the insurance pays part of it.
Every October there is ‘Octobre rose’, a campaign for breast cancer screening (‘dépistage’). In many cases women from 50 are invited every two years.
b1-03: In winter there is a ban on evictions (‘trêve hivernale’), usually from 1 November to 31 March.
‘Logement social’ is also called ‘HLM’. You make a request online and often wait a long time in big cities.
Landlords often ask for a ‘garant’ (a person who guarantees the rent). The state-backed guarantee ‘Visale’ can replace it for some tenants.
b1-04: Foreign documents often need an ‘apostille’ and a translation by a sworn translator (‘traducteur assermenté’).
‘Une convocation’ is an official letter or message that tells you to come to an office at a set time. Bring your ID.
Many residence procedures for foreigners are done online on the ANEF platform.
b1-05: French degrees follow ‘LMD’: ‘licence’ (3 years), ‘master’ (2 more), ‘doctorat’ (3 more).
Gender trap: ‘un mémoire’ is a thesis, ‘la mémoire’ is memory, and ‘les Mémoires’ are memoirs.
False friend: ‘une conférence’ is a lecture or talk. A big meeting of experts is ‘un congrès’ or ‘un colloque’.
b1-06: Around two thirds of France's electricity comes from nuclear power plants, more than in most countries.
‘L'essence’ is petrol and ‘le gazole’ is diesel. ‘Le gaz’ is the gas for cooking and heating.
In some cities cars need a ‘Crit'Air’ sticker, which shows how much they pollute. Check the rules of your city.
b1-07: Income tax is taken from your pay each month (‘prélèvement à la source’, since 2019). You still file a tax return (‘déclaration de revenus’) once a year, usually online.
The standard VAT rate (‘TVA’) is 20 per cent. Some goods, for example many foods, have a lower rate.
A ‘découvert’ (overdraft) can be authorised or not. An unauthorised one usually costs high fees.
b1-08: ‘Un bouchon’ is a cork and also a traffic jam. ‘Un embouteillage’ means the same.
‘Bison Futé’ is the official traffic forecast. Its colours show how busy the roads will be on holiday days: green, orange, red, black.
A speed bump is ‘un dos d'âne’ (a donkey's back). ‘La rocade’ is a ring road around a town.
b1-09: False friend: ‘actuel’ means ‘current’, ‘actuellement’ means ‘at the moment’, not ‘actually’.
Many people watch ‘le journal de 20 heures’, the evening news at 8 pm on TF1 and France 2.
‘Ouest-France’ is one of the biggest newspapers in France and a regional one. The big national papers include ‘Le Monde’ and ‘Le Figaro’.
b1-10: Fillers that you will hear all the time: ‘euh’, ‘ben’, ‘bah’, ‘en fait’, ‘du coup’, ‘bref’.
‘Salutations’ is used at the end of a letter. In an email ‘Cordialement’ and ‘Bien à vous’ are common.
‘Une blague’ is a joke. ‘Tu plaisantes ?’ and ‘Tu rigoles ?’ mean ‘Are you joking?’.
b1-11: The motto of the French Republic is ‘Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité’. ‘Laïcité’ means that the state is neutral in religious matters.
‘Les Restos du Cœur’ is a well-known charity that gives free meals. The comedian Coluche founded it in 1985.
Abbreviations are often said letter by letter: ‘ONG’ is said ‘o-en-gé’.
b1-12: ‘Un avocat’ is a lawyer and also an avocado.
France's ‘Code civil’ dates from 1804 and is still the base of private law.
People with a low income can get legal aid (‘aide juridictionnelle’). Check service-public.fr.
b1-13: In French the order of abbreviations is often reversed: ‘IA’ for ‘intelligence artificielle’ (AI), ‘ADN’ for DNA, ‘OTAN’ for NATO.
‘Le numérique’ is the general word for digital technology. ‘Un logiciel’ is software.
The CNIL is the French authority for data protection. The EU rules are called ‘RGPD’ in French (GDPR in English).
b1-14: Clubs are usually ‘associations loi 1901’. You become an ‘adhérent’ and pay a ‘cotisation’.
In early September many towns hold a ‘forum des associations’, where you can meet clubs and sign up.
‘Un concours’ is a competition and also a competitive entrance exam.
b1-15: ‘Bon voyage !’ is for a journey. For someone going by car you can say ‘Bonne route !’.
The main Paris airports are Roissy-Charles-de-Gaulle and Orly.
France has more time zones than any other country because of its overseas territories. In mainland France it is one hour ahead of GMT in winter.
b1-16: ‘Un régime’ means a diet (‘être au régime’), and also a political regime or a bunch of bananas.
‘Nutri-Score’ is a colour label from A (green) to E (red) on many food packs. It was created in France.
A law from 2016 forbids large supermarkets to destroy unsold food that is still good. They must give it away, for example to charities.
b1-17: ‘Un expatrié’ is often someone sent abroad by a company. ‘Un immigré’ is the official statistical word. The two words feel different.
New arrivals from outside the EU often sign a ‘contrat d'intégration républicaine’ with OFII, with a language test and civic training.
‘Avoir le mal du pays’ means to feel homesick.
b1-18: The President is elected directly for five years (the ‘quinquennat’ since 2002) in two rounds.
There are 577 members of the Assemblée nationale (‘députés’). With the Sénat they make up ‘le Parlement’.
Elections in France are held on Sundays. Municipal elections take place every six years.
b1-19: Unemployment benefit (‘ARE’) is paid through France Travail, the public employment service. It was called Pôle emploi until 2024.
‘Un commerce’ is a shop or small business: ‘les commerces de proximité’ are local shops.
‘Le CAC 40’ is the main index of the Paris stock exchange.
b1-20: Every year in September, on the ‘Journées européennes du patrimoine’, many monuments and official buildings open their doors for free.
‘Le patrimoine’ means both heritage and a person's wealth. ‘Le patrimoine culturel’ is cultural heritage.
A ‘vernissage’ is the opening of an art show. It is usually open to everyone, often with a drink.
b1-21: ‘Penser à’ is to think of someone (‘Je pense à toi’). ‘Penser de’ asks for an opinion: ‘Que penses-tu de ce film ?’.
‘Un souvenir’ is a memory and also a souvenir. ‘Se souvenir de’ means to remember.
‘Faire confiance à quelqu'un’ means to trust someone. ‘Avoir confiance en soi’ is to be self-confident.
b1-22: ‘Un os’ is said ‘oss’, but ‘des os’ is said ‘o’: the -s disappears in the plural.
‘Un genou’ has the plural ‘des genoux’ with -x, like ‘un caillou’ and ‘un chou’.
‘Je me suis foulé la cheville’ means ‘I sprained my ankle’. ‘Un pouce’ is a thumb and also an inch.
b1-23: ‘Beau-père’ and ‘belle-mère’ mean both father-in-law and stepfather, mother-in-law and stepmother.
‘Une crèche’ is a day nursery for small children and also a nativity scene at Christmas.
In France a civil wedding at the town hall is required. A religious ceremony has no legal effect. The ‘PACS’ is a civil partnership open to all couples.
b1-24: In many supermarkets you need a coin or a token to take a trolley (‘un chariot’). You get it back when you return it.
On the shelf the price per kilo or litre must be shown (‘prix au kilo’), which helps you compare.
Bakeries and markets are often open on Sunday morning. Many other shops are closed on Sunday.
b1-25: Paris is divided into 20 ‘arrondissements’ that spiral from the centre. ‘Le 15e’ means the 15th arrondissement.
Many towns have a ‘rue de la République’, a ‘place de la mairie’ and an ‘avenue Charles-de-Gaulle’.
‘Banlieue’ simply means suburbs, but the word often carries a social image.
b1-26: ‘Un fleuve’ flows into the sea. ‘Une rivière’ flows into another river. The Loire is the longest river in France.
‘Une côte’ means a coast, a slope, a rib and a chop: ‘une côte de porc’.
Mont Blanc, in the Alps, is the highest mountain in Western Europe, about 4,800 m.
b1-27: Météo-France uses four warning colours, called ‘vigilance’: green, yellow, orange and red.
‘Il pleut des cordes’ means ‘it is pouring’ (literally: it rains ropes).
‘Un éclair’ is a flash of lightning and also a pastry.
b1-28: The Académie française, founded in 1635, publishes a dictionary and gives advice. Its advice is not law.
French has accent marks: ‘é’ (aigu), ‘è’ (grave), ‘ê’ (circonflexe), ‘ç’ (cédille) and ‘ë’ (tréma). They can change the meaning: ‘a’ and ‘à’, ‘ou’ and ‘où’.
Around 300 million people speak French in the world. ‘La francophonie’ is the name for all French-speaking countries and communities.
b1-29: False friend: ‘un costume’ is a man's suit. A costume for a party is ‘un déguisement’.
‘Des lunettes’ (glasses) is always plural: ‘une paire de lunettes’.
‘Haute couture’ is a protected term in France. Only a few fashion houses may use it.
b1-30: Centuries are written in Roman numerals: ‘le XXIe siècle’ (le vingt et unième siècle).
Official times use the 24-hour clock: ‘dix-sept heures trente’. In daily speech people say ‘cinq heures et demie’.
b1-31: The metric system comes from France. It was created at the time of the French Revolution.
Marie Curie, born in Poland, worked in Paris and won two Nobel Prizes (1903 and 1911).
‘Le CNRS’ is the largest public research organisation in France.
b1-32: Salaries are often quoted ‘brut’ (gross). The ‘net’ (what you receive before income tax) is usually clearly lower, often around three quarters.
‘Le treizième mois’ is an extra month's pay at the end of the year. It is not a legal rule: it depends on the company or the collective agreement.
‘Un cadre’ is a status of managers and higher employees, with its own rules, for example on working time.
b1-33: ‘Un aide-soignant’ helps patients with care, while ‘un infirmier’ is a nurse. They are two different jobs.
‘Une radio’ is short for ‘radiographie’ (X-ray). ‘Un scanner’ is a CT scan, and ‘une IRM’ is an MRI scan.
A single room (‘chambre individuelle’) often costs extra. Many ‘mutuelles’ cover part of it.
b1-34: ‘Linky’ is the name of the smart electricity meter that most homes in France have.
‘Une moquette’ is a fitted carpet, ‘un tapis’ is a rug.
The TV licence fee (‘redevance audiovisuelle’) was abolished in 2022.
b1-35: The CAF (Caisse d'allocations familiales) pays housing aid (‘APL’), family allowances and other benefits. It is not the same office as the health insurance.
‘France Services’ offices help you with online forms and official letters, for free.
If a benefit is refused you can ask for a review (‘recours’). The time limit is often two months, so look at the letter.
b1-36: School marks are out of 20 and 10 is the pass mark (‘la moyenne’). 20 out of 20 is very rare.
At the ‘collège’ the years count down: ‘la sixième’, ‘la cinquième’, ‘la quatrième’, ‘la troisième’. Then come ‘la seconde’, ‘la première’ and ‘la terminale’.
With the bac you can get a ‘mention’: ‘assez bien’, ‘bien’ or ‘très bien’.
b1-37: ‘Le Livret A’ is a popular, tax-free savings account. The state sets the interest rate.
The state pension works by ‘répartition’: today's workers pay for today's pensioners.
‘Boucler les fins de mois’ means to get through to the end of the month with your money.
b1-38: Every car in France must carry a high-visibility vest (‘gilet jaune’) and a warning triangle.
Cars need a ‘contrôle technique’ (a technical check) about every two years once they are older than four years.
A helmet (‘casque’) is compulsory for motorbike and scooter riders and for children under 12 on a bike.
b1-39: ‘Infox’ is the official French word for fake news. ‘Fake news’ is also used.
‘Les faits divers’ are the small news items about accidents and crimes. It is a typical French news category.
Fact-checking teams in newspapers, for example ‘Les Décodeurs’ at Le Monde, check claims.
b1-40: ‘Pardon ?’ means ‘Sorry, what did you say?’. ‘Pardon’ and ‘Excusez-moi’ are also used to get past someone.
‘Un compromis’ is a compromise and also the first contract when you buy a home: ‘le compromis de vente’.
Free ‘conciliateurs de justice’ help neighbours or small businesses to settle a dispute without going to court.
b1-41: ‘Bénévole’ is an unpaid volunteer. The word ‘volontaire’ often means someone with a paid civic service.
The ‘Banques alimentaires’ hold a big national collection of food every year, usually at the end of November.
Gifts to charities can reduce your income tax, often by around two thirds of the amount, up to a limit.
b1-42: French law has three levels of offence: ‘contravention’ (minor), ‘délit’ and ‘crime’ (the most serious).
Police work in towns (‘police nationale’). In rural areas the ‘gendarmerie’ is in charge. Many towns also have a ‘police municipale’.
To report a theft, ‘porter plainte’ at a ‘commissariat’ or a ‘gendarmerie’. You can often start the complaint online.
b1-43: ‘Un tournevis’ is literally ‘turn-screw’. The plural is the same: ‘des tournevis’.
‘Une pince’ is one pair of pliers. French uses the singular where English uses a plural.
‘Outil’ is said ‘outi’: the final -l is silent.
b1-44: Long-distance hiking paths are called ‘GR’ (grande randonnée) and are marked with red and white stripes.
‘Des baskets’ are sneakers. ‘Le basket’ is basketball.
In dry summers open fires in forests are often forbidden. Check the local rules before a ‘feu de camp’.
b1-45: Distances are often given in time: ‘C'est à dix minutes à pied’.
‘Une consigne’ is a left-luggage place or an instruction: ‘les consignes de sécurité’.
At a roundabout: ‘Au rond-point, prenez la deuxième sortie’.
b1-46: ‘Un couvert’ is a place setting (knife, fork and spoon). A table ‘de quatre couverts’ is a table for four people.
‘Fait maison’ is an official label for dishes cooked on site, from raw ingredients.
Many restaurant kitchens close in the afternoon, often at 2 pm, and reopen in the evening.
b2-01: ‘Un cadre’ is a manager or a professional with a certain status, and not only a senior boss.
Common job abbreviations: ‘PDG’ (président-directeur général), ‘DG’ (directeur général), ‘DRH’ (directeur des ressources humaines).
‘Les effectifs’ is always plural and means the number of staff of a company.
b2-02: ‘Mondialisation’ is the usual French word for globalisation. ‘Globalisation’ is used less.
False friend: ‘un concurrent’ is a competitor. ‘La concurrence’ is competition.
France defends the ‘exception culturelle’ in trade talks: films and books should not be treated like any other goods.
b2-03: ‘Caution’ means a deposit, a guarantee and a guarantor: ‘se porter caution’ is to act as a guarantor for someone.
‘Dommages et intérêts’ (damages) is nearly always plural.
The contract law of the Code civil was reformed in 2016.
b2-04: The Assemblée nationale meets in the Palais Bourbon, the Sénat in the Palais du Luxembourg. There are around 350 senators, elected indirectly.
With ‘l'article 49.3’ the government can pass a bill without a vote, unless the Assemblée passes a ‘motion de censure’.
The ‘Conseil constitutionnel’ checks whether a law respects the Constitution.
b2-05: ‘L'ascenseur social’ (the social lift) is a common image for social mobility. People say ‘l'ascenseur social est en panne’.
The ‘recensement’ by INSEE is not done in one year. Each year a part of the communes is counted.
‘L'État-providence’ is the welfare state, literally ‘the providence state’.
b2-06: The Paris Agreement on climate was adopted in 2015 at the ‘COP21’ in Paris.
A rise of the fuel tax (‘taxe carbone’) in 2018 was one of the triggers of the ‘gilets jaunes’ protests.
France has set the goal of ‘neutralité carbone’ by 2050.
b2-07: ‘Hameçonnage’ is the French word for phishing (‘hameçon’ is a fish hook). The site cybermalveillance.gouv.fr helps victims.
The correct word is ‘chiffrement’. ‘Cryptage’ is common but many experts avoid it.
b2-08: False friend: ‘une expérience’ is an experience and also an experiment.
‘Les données’ (data) is plural in French: ‘Les données sont fiables’.
French typography puts a space before the percent sign: ‘50 %’, and a comma for decimals: ‘3,5 %’.
b2-09: ‘Le Canard enchaîné’ is a satirical weekly paper, founded in 1915, known for its investigations.
The press law of 29 July 1881 guarantees the freedom of the press and also defines ‘diffamation’.
‘Un chroniqueur’ writes a regular column (‘une chronique’) or speaks on radio and TV.
b2-10: ‘Parcoursup’ is the national website for applications to first-year courses in higher education. ‘Mon Master’ is the one for master's programmes.
France has universities and also ‘grandes écoles’, which are highly selective schools. Many students enter them after ‘classes préparatoires’.
The ‘Crous’ runs student housing (‘résidence universitaire’) and cheap student restaurants (‘restos U’).
b2-11: Eleven vaccines are compulsory for children born since 2018.
‘Une flambée’ is an outbreak (literally a blaze): ‘une flambée de cas’.
‘Mois sans tabac’ is a yearly campaign in November that helps people to stop smoking.
b2-12: A ‘psychiatre’ is a doctor and a ‘psychologue’ is not. The rules for reimbursement differ. Check ameli.fr, for example for ‘MonParcoursPsy’.
‘3114’ is the national number for suicide prevention in France. It is free and open day and night.
‘Une dépression’ also means a low-pressure area in weather forecasts.
b2-13: Asylum applications are handled by the OFPRA. If a claim is refused you can appeal to the CNDA, a special court.
‘Un sans-papiers’ is a person without legal residence papers, literally ‘without papers’.
The Geneva Convention of 1951 defines who is a refugee.
b2-14: The plural of ‘chef-d'œuvre’ is ‘chefs-d'œuvre’: only the first part changes.
‘Le mécénat’ (patronage of the arts) gives companies and private people tax advantages.
‘Une toile’ is a canvas, that is a painting, and also a web: ‘la toile’ is an old word for the Internet.
b2-15: French has three main registers: ‘courant’ (standard), ‘familier’ (informal) and ‘soutenu’ (formal). ‘Argot’ is slang.
‘Technicien de surface’ is a soft word (a euphemism) for a cleaner: ‘agent d'entretien’.
b2-16: A ‘permis de construire’ comes from the town hall. The ‘PLU’ (plan local d'urbanisme) says what may be built where.
The ‘loi SRU’ asks many towns to have a share of social housing, often 20 or 25 per cent.
‘Une ville-dortoir’ is a dormitory town: people live there and work somewhere else.
b2-17: France has eleven national parks. The first one, la Vanoise, dates from 1963.
‘Un parc naturel régional’ is different: people live and work in it.
‘Le bocage’ is a landscape with fields and hedges, typical of western France.
b2-18: ‘L'assurance-vie’ is the most popular savings product in France. It is an investment wrapper, not only an insurance for death.
‘Une succession’ means an inheritance, and a notary (‘notaire’) usually handles it.
A ‘PEA’ (plan d'épargne en actions) is a special account for investing in shares, with tax advantages.
b2-19: The first TGV line, Paris–Lyon, opened in 1981.
‘Un nid-de-poule’ is a pothole, literally ‘a hen's nest’.
The Millau Viaduct in southern France, opened in 2004, is among the tallest bridges in the world.
b2-20: ‘Le silence vaut acceptation’: in many cases, when the administration does not answer within two months, this means yes. There are many exceptions.
‘Le Défenseur des droits’ is an independent authority you can contact for free if you think an office has treated you unfairly.
There are three kinds of appeal: ‘recours gracieux’ (to the same office), ‘recours hiérarchique’ (to the superior), ‘recours contentieux’ (to a court).
b2-21: ‘Le droit de retrait’ allows employees to stop work if they have a serious reason to think it is dangerous.
After an accident at work (‘accident du travail’) you must tell your employer quickly, usually within 24 hours.
‘Une astreinte’ is on-call time at home. It is paid differently from normal working time.
b2-22: ‘DLC’ (date limite de consommation) is a safety date: do not eat after it. ‘DDM’ (date de durabilité minimale) is ‘à consommer de préférence avant’: quality only.
The government site ‘Rappel Conso’ lists product recalls.
b2-23: ‘Un maillot’ is a jersey. ‘Le maillot jaune’ is worn by the leader of the Tour de France.
To play in a club you take a ‘licence’ with the sports federation: ‘prendre sa licence’.
‘Ligue 1’ is the top football league in France. ‘Top 14’ is the top rugby league.
b2-24: Family allowances (‘allocations familiales’) are paid from the second child, and their amount depends on income.
The tax system uses the ‘quotient familial’: the household is counted in ‘parts’, which depend on the number of people.
b2-25: The Ferry laws of 1881 and 1882 made primary school free, secular and compulsory.
School is compulsory from age 3 since 2019. ‘L'éducation prioritaire’ gives more help to schools in poorer areas.
Each August families on a low income can receive the ‘allocation de rentrée scolaire’.
b2-26: ‘Un bras de fer’ (arm wrestling) is a test of strength in a negotiation.
Haggling is not usual in shops. At a flea market (‘brocante’) you can try to bargain: ‘marchander’.
‘Certes… mais…’ (granted… but…) is a typical way to admit a point, then give your objection.
b2-27: Gender trap: ‘le moral’ is morale (‘avoir le moral’), ‘la morale’ is morality.
‘Pairs’, ‘père’, ‘paire’ and ‘perds’ sound the same. ‘La pression des pairs’ means peer pressure.
A proverb about procrastination: ‘Il ne faut pas remettre à demain ce qu'on peut faire aujourd'hui.’
b2-28: ‘Une pub’ (feminine) is an ad. ‘Un pub’ (masculine) is a bar of British type.
The ‘loi Évin’ of 1991 limits advertising for alcohol and tobacco.
A law of 2023 sets rules for influencers (‘influenceurs’), for example about marking paid posts.
b2-29: ‘EDF’ produces and sells electricity, ‘RTE’ runs the high-voltage grid and ‘Enedis’ the local network.
The tidal power plant on the river Rance in Brittany opened in 1966, and it was the first big one in the world.
‘L'EPR de Flamanville’ is a nuclear reactor that was connected to the grid in 2024, after many years of delay.
b2-30: ‘Micro-entrepreneur’ (before 2016 ‘auto-entrepreneur’) is a simple status for small businesses.
‘CA’ means both ‘chiffre d'affaires’ (turnover) and ‘conseil d'administration’ (board). Context tells you which.
Since 2023 company formalities are made through the ‘guichet unique’ on the website of the state.
b2-31: You can write ‘directives anticipées’ (advance directives) and name a ‘personne de confiance’ who speaks for you if you cannot.
The ‘loi Kouchner’ of 2002 gave patients more rights, for example to see their medical file.
As of 2026 euthanasia is not legal in France under current law. The question is under public debate, so check current news.
b2-32: ‘FR-Alert’ sends alerts to mobile phones in a danger zone.
‘Le plan ORSEC’ is the framework for emergency organisation by the state.
After a flood or storm the state can declare ‘un état de catastrophe naturelle’, which allows insurance payments (‘CatNat’).
b2-33: ‘Lanceur d'alerte’ is a whistleblower. They have legal protection under the ‘loi Sapin II’ of 2016.
The ‘HATVP’ (Haute Autorité pour la transparence de la vie publique) checks the declarations of assets of high officials.
The idea of ‘séparation des pouvoirs’ comes from Montesquieu, ‘De l'esprit des lois’ (1748).
b2-34: For a child in danger you can call 119, the national child protection line, free and open day and night.
For someone sleeping outside the number 115 (‘SAMU social’) helps to find emergency housing.
‘Le CCAS’ (centre communal d'action sociale) is the social office of a town hall.
b2-35: ‘Passeport talent’ is a multi-year residence permit for skilled workers and other groups.
To have a foreign diploma compared with French ones, you can ask France Éducation international (ENIC-NARIC) for an ‘attestation de comparabilité’ (a certificate).
‘Les métiers en tension’ are jobs where employers find it hard to recruit. There is an official list.
b2-36: ‘Le Quai d'Orsay’ is a nickname for the ministry of foreign affairs, after its address in Paris.
France is one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council with a right of veto.
‘OTAN’ is NATO. France left NATO's integrated command in 1966 and came back in 2009.
b2-37: Research on people usually needs approval by an ethics committee, for example a ‘comité de protection des personnes’.
France has an ‘Office français de l'intégrité scientifique’, created in 2017.
‘Consentement éclairé’ (informed consent) means the person understood the risks before agreeing.
b2-38: Tap water in France is among the most closely checked foods. ‘L'eau du robinet’ is drinkable almost everywhere.
France has six ‘agences de l'eau’ that manage the water of big river basins.
The water bill includes the cost of ‘assainissement’ (collecting and cleaning waste water).
b2-39: The Cannes Film Festival takes place every May. Its top prize is the ‘Palme d'or’.
‘Une tournée’ is a tour and also a round of drinks: ‘C'est ma tournée !’.
‘Bis !’ is what an audience shouts to ask for an encore.
b2-40: Since 2019 French law forbids physical punishment of children (‘fessée’) in the family.
Since 2021 the paternity leave (‘congé paternité’) is longer than before, around a month. Check service-public.fr for the details.
b2-41: ‘Denim’ comes from ‘de Nîmes’, a town in southern France.
‘Une griffe’ is a designer label, and also a claw.
‘Une friperie’ is a second-hand clothes shop. There are also ‘vide-dressings’, where people sell their clothes.
b2-42: Météo-France gives names to big storms. For example storm ‘Alex’ in 2020.
On 11 to 13 May the ‘Saints de glace’ are said to bring a last cold spell. It is a folk belief.
‘Les intempéries’ is always plural and means bad weather.
b2-43: ‘Le legs’ (a legacy) is said ‘lè’ or ‘lèg’. Both pronunciations are accepted.
The ‘livret de famille’ is a small booklet where births, marriages and deaths of a family are recorded.
b2-44: ‘J'en ai marre’ and ‘J'en ai ras-le-bol’ mean ‘I have had enough’.
‘Avoir le cafard’ (literally ‘to have the cockroach’) means to feel down.
‘Une jalousie’ is a jealousy and also a slatted window shutter.
b2-45: The ‘DGCCRF’ is the consumer authority. The website ‘SignalConso’ lets you report problems with a shop.
Prices are shown ‘TTC’ (toutes taxes comprises, VAT included) to consumers and ‘HT’ (hors taxes) between companies.
‘Les soldes’ are regulated by law and take place twice a year, in winter and in summer.
b2-46: ‘Avoir la main verte’ (to have a green hand) means to be good with plants.
‘Un talon’ is a heel and also the stub of a ticket or a cheque.
b2-47: ‘Huit jours’ means one week and ‘quinze jours’ means two weeks.
‘Dans deux jours’ means in two days' time. ‘En deux jours’ means within two days: it takes two days.
‘Une date butoir’ is a deadline. ‘Un butoir’ is a buffer stop, like at the end of a railway track.
b2-48: A European rule gives passengers the right to help and sometimes to compensation when a flight is cancelled or very late.
‘Une franchise de bagages’ is the allowed weight. In insurance ‘une franchise’ is the amount you pay yourself.
The European Health Insurance Card (‘CEAM’) can be requested for free through ameli.fr for a trip in Europe.
b2-49: The ‘frais de notaire’ are around 7 to 8 per cent of the price for older homes, and mostly consist of taxes.
After signing the ‘compromis de vente’ the buyer usually has ten days to withdraw (‘délai de rétractation’).
‘La taxe foncière’ is paid by owners every year. The ‘taxe d'habitation’ was abolished for main homes.
b2-50: The spire (‘flèche’) of Notre-Dame de Paris burned in April 2019. The cathedral reopened in December 2024.
‘Haussmannien’ describes the wide boulevards and cream-coloured buildings of Paris from the 19th century.
Changes near a listed monument (‘monument historique’) usually need the approval of an ‘architecte des Bâtiments de France’.
b2-51: Citizens of other EU countries who live in France can vote in local and European elections once they are on the electoral list.
‘Une procuration’ lets another person vote for you if you cannot go. You can start it online.
When you vote, the person at the table says ‘A voté !’ after you put your envelope in the box.
b2-52: False friend: ‘vulgariser’ means to explain science in a simple way (‘la vulgarisation scientifique’), not to make it vulgar.
The ‘Fête de la science’ takes place every autumn in labs and museums.
‘Complotisme’ is the belief in conspiracy theories (‘théories du complot’).
b2-53: INSEE is the national statistics office. ‘PIB’ (produit intérieur brut) is the GDP.
‘Le pouvoir d'achat’ (purchasing power) is a big topic in French public debate.
A ‘demandeur d'emploi’ is a person registered with France Travail as looking for work.
b2-54: ‘Un prévenu’ is a person tried for a ‘délit’. For a ‘crime’, before a ‘cour d'assises’, the person is called ‘un accusé’.
‘La garde à vue’ is police custody: usually up to 24 hours, which can be extended. The person has the right to a lawyer.
False friend: ‘une audience’ is a court hearing, not an audience at a theatre (that is ‘le public’).
b2-55: Since 1 January 2024 every household should be able to sort food waste (‘biodéchets’) at source.
Many households pay a waste tax (‘TEOM’) together with the property tax.
‘Encombrants’ (bulky items) can be taken to the ‘déchèterie’ or collected on request.
b2-56: ‘Un examen blanc’ is a mock exam, literally a ‘white exam’.
‘La correction’ means both the marking and the model answers: ‘Voici la correction’.
DELF and DALF diplomas for learners of French are valid for life: they do not expire.
b2-57: ‘Mistral AI’ is a French AI company founded in Paris in 2023.
‘Agent conversationnel’ is the official word for chatbot. ‘Hypertrucage’ is the official word for deepfake.
‘Le matériel’ is hardware and ‘le logiciel’ software.
b2-58: ‘Un abonné’ is a subscriber and also a follower. ‘S'abonner’ is to follow or subscribe.
‘Mot-dièse’ is the official French word for hashtag (‘dièse’ is the sharp sign #).
‘3018’ is a free number and app for children and teenagers who are victims of online harassment.
b2-59: A meeting usually has an ‘ordre du jour’ (agenda) and ‘questions diverses’ at the end. ‘Un tour de table’ lets everybody speak.
Spelling trap: ‘un différend’ (a dispute, with -d) and ‘différent’ (different).
‘La Réunion’ is a French island in the Indian Ocean. ‘Une réunion’ is a meeting.
b2-60: False friends: ‘attendre’ means to wait (not to attend), ‘assister à’ means to attend, ‘une librairie’ is a bookshop.
A famous tongue twister: ‘Les chaussettes de l'archiduchesse sont-elles sèches, archi-sèches ?’
Article 2 of the French Constitution says that the language of the Republic is French.
